289: Witness, Heaven, how often I lie down in my bed with a wish, and even a hope, that I may never wake again.
And in the morning, when I open my eyes, I see the sun once more, and I am wretched.
If I were whimsical, I might blame the weather, or an acquaintance, or some personal disappointment for my discontent; and then this unbearable load of trouble would not rest entirely on me.
But alas, I feel it too sadly.
I alone am the cause of my own misery, am I not?
Truly, my own breast holds the source of all my sorrow, as it once held the source of all my pleasure.
Am I not the same creature who once enjoyed an excess of happiness, who at every step saw paradise open before him, and whose heart went out to the whole world?
And that heart is dead now; no feeling can revive it.
My eyes are dry; and my senses, no longer refreshed by soft tears, wither and burn up my brain.
I suffer greatly, for I have lost the one charm of life: that active, sacred power which created worlds around me is gone.

When I look from my window at the distant hills and see the morning sun breaking through the mist and lighting up the country, still wrapped in silence, while the soft stream winds gently through the willows that have shed their leaves;

when glorious nature spreads all her beauties before me, and her wondrous prospects cannot draw one tear of joy from my withered heart, I feel that I stand at such a moment like a reprobate before heaven — hardened, insensible, unmoved.
Often then I bend my knee to the earth and beg God for the blessing of tears, as a despairing labourer in some scorching country prays for the dews of heaven to wet his parched corn.
290: But I feel that God does not grant sunshine or rain to our importunate entreaties.
And oh, those days gone by, whose memory now torments me — why were they so happy?
Because I waited then with patience for the blessings of the Eternal, and received his gifts with the gratitude of a thankful heart.
292: Charlotte has rebuked me for my excesses, and with such tenderness and goodness!
I have lately been drinking more wine than I used to.
"Think of you!" I answered. "Need you tell me to do that?"
"Think of you — I do not think of you: you are always before my soul."
"This very morning I sat on the spot where, a few days ago, you stepped down from the carriage, and —"
She changed the subject at once, to stop me going any further.
My dear friend, my energies are all laid low: she can do with me whatever she pleases.
294: I thank you, Wilhelm, for your warm sympathy and your excellent advice; and I beg you to be quiet.
Leave me to my sufferings.
In spite of my wretchedness, I still have strength enough to endure.
I revere religion — you know I do.
I feel that it can give strength to the feeble and comfort to the afflicted; but does it affect all men equally?
Consider this vast universe: you will see thousands for whom it has never existed, thousands for whom it never will, whether it is preached to them or not.
And must it then necessarily exist for me?
Does not the Son of God himself say that those are his whom the Father has given him?
What if I have not been given to him?
What if the Father means to keep me for himself, as my heart sometimes suggests?
I beg you, do not misread this.
Do not draw derision out of my harmless words.
I am pouring out my whole soul before you.
Silence would otherwise be better for me; but I need not shrink from a subject that few know more about than I do myself.
What is the destiny of man but to fill up the measure of his sufferings and drink his allotted cup of bitterness?
And if that same cup was bitter to the God of heaven in human form, why should I put on a foolish pride and call it sweet?
Why should I be ashamed of shrinking at that fearful moment, when my whole being will tremble between existence and annihilation;
when the memory of the past, like a flash of lightning, will light up the dark gulf of what is to come; when everything dissolves around me and the whole world vanishes away?

Is this not the voice of a creature pressed beyond all resource, failing in itself, about to plunge into inevitable destruction, and groaning deeply at its own inadequate strength: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"
And should I be ashamed to use the same words?
Should I not shudder at a prospect that held its fears even for him who folds up the heavens like a garment?
296: She does not feel, she does not know, that she is preparing a poison which will destroy us both; and I drink deep of the draught that is to be my destruction.
What is the meaning of those kind looks she so often — often? no, not often, but sometimes — turns on me?
Or of the complacency with which she hears the involuntary feelings that so often escape me, and the tender pity for my suffering that shows in her face?
297: Yesterday, when I took my leave, she seized me by the hand and said, "Adieu, dear Werther."
It was the first time she ever called me dear, and the sound sank deep into my heart.
I have repeated it a hundred times; and last night, going to bed and talking to myself about this and that, I suddenly said, "Good night, dear Werther!" — and then could not help laughing at myself.
299: I cannot pray, "Leave her to me!" — and yet she often seems to belong to me.
I cannot pray, "Give her to me!" — for she is another man's.
In this way I make a joke of my troubles; and if I had the time, I could compose a whole litany of such antitheses.
301: She is aware of my sufferings.
This morning her look pierced my very soul.
I found her alone, and she was silent; she looked at me steadily.
I no longer saw in her face the charms of beauty or the fire of genius: those had gone.
But I was struck by an expression far more touching — a look of the deepest sympathy and the softest pity.
Why was I afraid to throw myself at her feet?
Why did I not dare take her in my arms and answer her with a thousand kisses?
She turned to her piano for relief, and in a low, sweet voice accompanied the music with delicious sounds.
Her lips never looked so lovely: they seemed just to open, so as to drink in the sweet tones coming from the instrument and send the heavenly vibration back from her lovely mouth.
Oh, who can express what I felt?
I was quite overcome, and bending down I made this vow: "Beautiful lips, which the angels guard, never will I try to profane your purity with a kiss."
And yet, my friend — oh, I wish — but my heart is darkened with doubt and indecision — if I could only taste that happiness, and then die to atone for the sin!
303: Often I say to myself: "You alone are wretched; every other mortal is happy, and nobody is distressed as you are."
Then I read a passage in some ancient poet, and I seem to be reading my own heart.
I have so much to endure!
Have men before me ever been so wretched?
305: I shall never be myself again!
Wherever I go, some fatality happens to distract me.
Even today — alas for our destiny, alas for human nature!
306: About dinner time I went to walk by the riverside, having no appetite.
Everything around seemed gloomy; a cold, damp easterly wind blew from the mountains, and black, heavy clouds spread over the plain.
At a distance I noticed a man in a tattered coat, wandering among the rocks and seeming to look for plants.
When I came nearer he turned round at the noise, and I saw he had an interesting face, whose chief feature was a settled melancholy strongly marked with benevolence.
His long black hair was parted and fell over his shoulders.
As his clothes marked him as a man of the lower orders, I thought he would not take it badly if I asked about his business, and so I asked what he was looking for.
He answered with a deep sigh that he was looking for flowers, and could find none.
"But it is not the season," I said, with a smile.
"Oh, there are so many flowers!" he answered, coming closer to me.
"In my garden there are roses and honeysuckles of two kinds; one kind my father gave me. They grow as thick as weeds."
"I have been looking for them these two days, and cannot find them."
"There are flowers out there — yellow, blue, and red; and that centaury has a very pretty blossom. But I can find none of them."
I noticed his oddity, and so asked him, with an air of indifference, what he meant to do with his flowers.
A strange smile spread over his face.
Holding a finger to his mouth, he expressed a hope that I would not betray him, and then told me he had promised to gather a nosegay for his mistress.
"That is right," said I.
"Oh," he replied, "she has many other things besides: she is very rich."
"And yet," I went on, "she likes your nosegays."
"Oh, she has jewels and crowns!" he exclaimed.
I asked who she was.
"If the states-general would only pay me," he added, "I should be quite another man."
"Alas, there was a time when I was so happy; but that is past, and now I am —"
He raised his swimming eyes to heaven.
"And you were happy once?" I said.
"Ah, would I were so still!" was his answer.
"I was as gay and contented then as a man can be."
An old woman coming toward us now called out, "Henry, Henry! Where are you?"
"We have been looking for you everywhere. Come to dinner."
"Is he your son?" I asked, going over to her.
"Yes," she said, "he is my poor, unfortunate son."
"The Lord has sent me a heavy affliction."
I asked whether he had been long in this state.
She answered, "He has been as calm as he is now for about six months."
"I thank Heaven that he has come so far: he was raving for a whole year, and chained down in a madhouse."
"Now he harms nobody, but talks of nothing except kings and queens."
"He used to be a very good, quiet lad, and helped to keep me; he wrote a very fine hand."
"But all at once he turned melancholy, was seized with a violent fever, went out of his mind, and is now as you see him."
"If I were only to tell you, sir —"
I interrupted her by asking what period it was that he boasted of having been so happy in.
"Poor boy!" she cried, with a smile of compassion. "He means the time when he was completely deranged — a time he never stops regretting, when he was in the madhouse and knew nothing of anything."
I was thunderstruck. I put a piece of money into her hand and hurried away.
307: "You were happy!" I exclaimed, as I hurried back toward the town. "As gay and contented as a man can be!"
God of heaven! Is this the destiny of man?
Is he only happy before he comes to his reason, or after he has lost it?
And yet I envy your fate; I envy the delusion you are the victim of.
You go out with joy to gather flowers for your princess — in winter — and grieve when you can find none, and cannot understand why they do not grow.
But I go out without joy, without hope, without design; and I come back as I went.
You imagine what a man you would be if the states-general paid you.
Happy mortal, who can put his wretchedness down to an earthly cause!
You do not know, you do not feel, that in your own distracted heart and disordered brain lies the source of a misery that all the potentates on earth could not relieve.
308: Let that man die unconsoled who can mock an invalid for making a journey to distant healing springs, where he often finds only a heavier disease and a more painful death.
Or who can gloat over the despairing mind of a sinner who, to win peace of conscience and some easing of his misery, makes a pilgrimage to the Holy Sepulchre.
Every laborious step that galls his wounded feet on rough and untrodden paths pours a drop of balm into his troubled soul, and each weary day's journey brings his anguished heart a night's relief.
Will you dare to call this enthusiasm, you crowd of pompous declaimers?
O God, you see my tears.
You have allotted us our portion of misery: must we have brothers to persecute us as well, to rob us of our consolation, of our trust in you and in your love and mercy?
For our trust in the virtue of the healing root, or in the strength of the vine — what is it but a belief in you, from whom everything around us draws its healing and restoring power?
Father, whom I do not know, who once used to fill my soul but now hide your face from me — call me back to you; be silent no longer.
Your silence will not hold back a soul that thirsts after you.

What man, what father, could be angry with a son for coming back to him suddenly, for falling on his neck and crying, "I am here again, my father! Forgive me if I have cut short my journey and come home before the appointed time!"
"The world is everywhere the same — a scene of labour and pain, of pleasure and reward; but what does all of it come to?"
"I am happy only where you are, and in your presence I am content to suffer or enjoy."
And would you, heavenly Father, drive such a child from your presence?
310: Wilhelm, the man I wrote to you about — the man so enviable in his misfortunes — was secretary to Charlotte's father.
An unhappy passion for her, which he nursed and hid and at last let show, was what got him dismissed from his post.
That was what drove him mad.
Think, as you read this plain account, what an impression the thing has made on me!
And it was told to me by Albert with as much calmness as you will probably read it with.
312: It is all over with me.
I cannot bear this state any longer.
Today I was sitting beside Charlotte.
She was playing a succession of delightful melodies on her piano, with such intense expression!
Her little sister was dressing her doll on my lap.
The tears came into my eyes.
I leaned down and looked hard at her wedding ring; my tears fell — and at once she began to play that favourite, that divine air which has so often enchanted me.
I drew comfort from the memory of the past, of the days gone by when that air was familiar to me; and then I recalled all the sorrows and disappointments I have endured since.
I paced the room with hasty strides, my heart convulsed with painful feelings.
At length I went up to her and cried out eagerly, "For Heaven's sake, play that air no longer!"
She stopped and looked steadily at me.
Then she said, with a smile that sank deep into my heart, "Werther, you are ill: your dearest food is distasteful to you."
"But go, I beg you, and try to compose yourself."
God, you see my torments, and you will end them.
314: Waking or sleeping, she fills my whole soul.
The moment I close my eyes, here in my brain, where all the nerves of sight come together, her dark eyes are printed.
Here — I do not know how to describe it; but if I shut my eyes, hers are before me at once, dark as an abyss, opening on me and swallowing my senses.
315: And what is man — that boasted demigod?
Do his powers not fail him just when he most needs to use them?
And whether he soars in joy or sinks in sorrow, is his flight not stopped in both?
And while he fondly dreams he is grasping at infinity, does he not feel himself forced back to a consciousness of his cold, monotonous existence?
